newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan pork export ban seen hitting jobs.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan pork export ban seen hitting jobs.

text.p: Taiwan's ban on pork exports will cost some jobs and cut into the country's overall export figure but otherwise have little impact on the economy, officials and economists said on Friday.
The cabinet-level Council of Agriculture said on Thursday that it was banning temporarily exports of fresh and frozen pork due to an outbreak of the deadly and contagious foot-and-mouth disease.
Japan and South Korea on Friday said they had banned pork imports from Taiwan indefinitely because of the disease.
"The ban on pork exports will hurt Taiwan's exports, increase the jobless rate, but should have little impact on our overall economy," said Nomura Securities economist Amy Huang.
"The trend of our slowly recovering economy should continue."
The council estimated that Taiwan exported six million of the 14 million hogs it bred per year.

According to an industry survey, the hog industry's total production value stood at T$89 billion (US$3.24 billion) in 1994, or 20 percent of Taiwan's farm market and 60 percent of the livestock sector.
The hog output accounted for 1.53 percent of Taiwan's 1994 gross domestic product of T$5.817 trillion.
Taiwan's pork exports totalled US$1.55 billion in 1996, 99.48 percent of which went to Japan, the Board of Foreign Trade said.

Pork exports accounted for 11.3 percent of Taiwan's exports to Japan, which reached US$13.67 billion in 1996. They represented 1.34 percent of the island's total exports, which totalled US$115.98 billion in 1996.
"The pork export ban will hit our exports to Japan, and worsen our trade deficit with Japan," said Weng Kuang-hwa, a director of the Board of Foreign Trade.
Taiwan had a trade deficit of US$13.83 billion with Japan in 1996.
The agriculture council said the directly employed work force in the hog industry was about 100,000, and some 700,000 in related industries.
Economists said the pork export ban may cost as many as 50,000 workers their jobs, which will add some 0.5-0.6 percentage points on the island's jobless rate.
Taiwan's unemployment rate in 1996 was 2.60 percent, a 10-year high.
"The jobless rate may rise to as much as 3.2 percent if we estimate half of the direct work force affected by the pork export ban," said Deniel Chen, chief economist at Chinatrust Commercial Bank.
But, he said, many of the workers in the hog industry considered their hog business as a part-time job and would turn to other businesses.
"The real impact will not be so big as we have anticipated," Chen said.

"The impact on the overall economy will be limited because we can use the original work force (in the hog industry) to generate other output, and we still have certain domestic demand for pork," he said. (US$1 = T$27.5)
